primary_claim: In a blinded red-team/blue-team auditing game with five model organisms (two sandbagging via password-locking, three benign), the blue team correctly classified only 1/5 models using black-box techniques and deception probes, and 2/5 after gaining fine-tuning access, while on-distribution fine-tuning with a single demonstration fully elicited all sandbagging models.

effect.metric: blue team detection accuracy (models correctly classified out of 5)
effect.value: Phase 1 (black-box + probes): 1/5 correct; Phase 2 (with fine-tuning access): 2/5 correct

contradicts_or_qualifies: prior work (arXiv:2410.21514) suggesting anti-refusal training could elicit sandbagging models; anti-refusal training failed to elicit their models
stated_future_work: design an auditing game where achieving harm robustly requires the model to have some self-conception of its goals/behavior
measure what kinds of tasks a model can execute without understanding what it is doing
investigate the efficacy of lie detection in the context of post-hoc interrogation and follow-up questions
extend detection and elicitation approaches to open-ended research tasks rather than capabilities evals
research whether training-based elicitation is practical and adversarially robust
limitations_stated: model organism realism relative to real-world scheming/sandbagging is uncertain
no quantitative guarantees: only ten model organisms and one blue team, so detection rates can't be statistically estimated
several post-hoc methods (SAEs, sandbagging probes, fuzzing) were only explored after unblinding
both sandbagging organisms were fine-tuned from the same base model (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct), limiting diversity
only benchmarks with checkable answers were tested; open-ended research tasks might be harder to audit
quote: The red team won. The blue team only classified 1/5 models correctly when using black-box techniques and deception probes, and 2/5 when they were subsequently given fine-tuning access.
